propositions.text: Mr. Muhammad Zeeshan is a Pakistani national residing in Pakistan, son of Mr. Muhammad Azam Qureshi who filed refugee claims in Canada.
propositions.quote: Mr. Muhammad Zeeshan, is a national of Pakistan who currently resides in Pakistan. His father, Mr. Muhammad Azam Qureshi, is also from Pakistan.

propositions.text: Mr. Qureshi filed refugee claims in 2017 and 2018; his claim was accepted in 2018 and he applied for permanent residence including his spouse and youngest son, Mr. Zeeshan.
propositions.quote: In 2017, Mr. Qureshi filed a first refugee claim in Canada, and submitted a second and updated one in 2018. His claim was accepted in 2018, at which point he applied for permanent residence and included his spouse and his youngest son, Mr. Zeeshan, in his application.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan was 24 when his father filed the refugee claim and 25 when included in the permanent residence application.
propositions.quote: Mr. Zeeshan was 24 years old when his father filed his refugee claim and 25 years old when he was included in his father’s application for permanent residence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Zeeshan is a Pakistani national, son of Mr. Qureshi who filed refugee claims accepted in 2018, including Mr. Zeeshan in permanent residence application.

propositions.text: On October 29, 2021, a procedural fairness letter informed the Applicants Mr. Zeeshan did not meet the definition of dependent child under IRPA due to age.
propositions.quote: On October 29, 2021, a procedural fairness letter was provided to the Applicants noting that, by virtue of his age, Mr. Zeeshan did not meet the definition of a “dependent child” under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

propositions.text: The letter invited the Applicants to provide information to support a request for consideration on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
propositions.quote: The letter invited the Applicants to provide information and evidence to support a request for consideration of the application on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds, should they wish.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a 2021 letter informed Mr. Zeeshan he was not a dependent child under IRPA and invited H&C grounds submissions.

propositions.text: Mr. Qureshi, spouse, and eight children are Ahmadi Muslims; Mr. Zeeshan highlighted his Canadian connection, religious freedom, and Ahmadis' situation in Pakistan in submissions.
propositions.quote: Mr. Qureshi, his spouse, and his eight children are Ahmadi Muslims. In his submissions, Mr. Zeeshan highlighted his connection to Canada through his parents, the freedom of religion in Canada, his circumstances in Pakistan, and the situation for Ahmadis in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the family are Ahmadi Muslims and Mr. Zeeshan emphasized his Canadian ties and Ahmadis' situation in Pakistan in submissions.

propositions.text: On April 27, 2022, an IRCC officer in London denied Mr. Zeeshan’s application, finding H&C considerations did not justify exemption from IRPA requirements.
propositions.quote: On April 27, 2022, an officer of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada in London, England [Officer] denied Mr. Zeeshan’s application on the basis that the H&C considerations did not justify granting him an exemption from the requirements of the IRPA [Decision].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the IRCC officer denied Mr. Zeeshan’s application in April 2022, finding H&C grounds insufficient for exemption.

propositions.text: The Officer erred by failing to explain treatment of systemic discrimination of Ahmadis.
propositions.quote: The Applicants assert that the Officer erred: (a) by failing to provide a reasoned explanation for the Officer’s treatment of the systemic discrimination of the Ahmadis;

propositions.text: The Officer erred in handling and weighing Mr. Zeeshan’s personal experience, especially considering his father’s experience.
propositions.quote: (b) in the handling and weighing of Mr. Zeeshan’s personal experience, especially in light of his father’s experience;

propositions.text: The Officer applied the wrong test and failed to consider all H&C factors.
propositions.quote: (c) by applying the wrong test and not considering all of the H&C factors in play.

paragraphs.summary: The applicants argue the Officer erred by failing to explain systemic discrimination, mishandling personal experience, and applying the wrong test.

propositions.text: The Officer acknowledged discrimination against Ahmadis but reasonably concluded exemption was not warranted considering all H&C factors.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that while the Officer specifically acknowledged that discrimination against the Ahmadi community occurs in Pakistan, he reasonably concluded, taking all the H&C factors into account, that an exemption was not warranted.

propositions.text: The Officer reasonably found Mr. Zeeshan has family support and financial support from parents in Canada and lives with siblings.
propositions.quote: The Respondent pleads that the Officer reasonably found that Mr. Zeeshan has family support as he can be financially supported by his parents from Canada and lives with his three older siblings.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Officer reasonably acknowledged discrimination but found exemption unwarranted given family and financial support.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application for judicial review is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The applicable standard of review is reasonableness as set out in Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The parties agree that the applicable standard of review is that of reasonableness as set out in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov]).

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is justified in relation to facts and law constraining the decision maker (Vavilov para 85).
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is justified in relation to the facts and the law that constrain the decision maker (Vavilov at para 85).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov, requiring justification related to facts and law.

propositions.text: Applicants bear the onus to show the Officer’s decision is unreasonable (Vavilov para 100).
propositions.quote: It is the Applicants who bear the onus of demonstrating that the Officer’s decision is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 100).

propositions.text: Court intervenes only if serious shortcomings make decision unjustified, unintelligible or non-transparent (Vavilov para 100).
propositions.quote: For the reviewing court to intervene, the challenging party must satisfy the court that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency”, and that such alleged shortcomings or flaws “must be more than merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision” (Vavilov at para 100).

propositions.text: A decision is unreasonable if reasons fail to reveal a rational chain of analysis (Vavilov para 103).
propositions.quote: As emphasized by Mr. Zeeshan during the hearing, “a decision will be unreasonable if the reasons for it, read holistically, fail to reveal a rational chain of analysis” (Vavilov at para 103).

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants must prove unreasonableness with serious shortcomings; Mr. Zeeshan argues decision lacks rational analysis.

propositions.text: Review focuses on decision made and justification, not court’s own conclusion (Vavilov para 125).
propositions.quote: The focus must be on the decision actually made, including the justification offered for it, and not the conclusion the Court itself would have reached in the administrative decision maker’s place.

propositions.text: Court should not interfere with factual findings absent exceptional circumstances and should not reweigh evidence (Vavilov para 125).
propositions.quote: A reviewing court should not interfere with factual findings, absent exceptional circumstances, and it is not the function of this Court on an application for judicial review to reweigh or reassess the evidence considered by the decision maker (Vavilov at para 125).

paragraphs.summary: The court states review focuses on decision and justification, not reweighing evidence or substituting conclusions.

propositions.text: Respondent argues affidavit paragraphs 3 and 4 should not be considered as not before the Officer.
propositions.quote: In their pleadings and at the outset of the hearing, the Respondent raised the issue that information contained in the affidavit of Shafia Bhatti dated December 19, 2022, specifically paragraphs 3 and 4, should not be considered on the basis that this information was not before the Officer.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues affidavit paragraphs 3 and 4 should be excluded as not before the Officer.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan submits affidavit information was included to assure the Court the matter is not moot.
propositions.quote: Mr. Zeeshan submits that the information was included to assure the Court that the matter is not moot.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Zeeshan submits affidavit information was to assure the Court the matter is not moot.

propositions.text: General rule: judicial review evidence limited to record before decision maker (Access Copyright para 19).
propositions.quote: The general rule is that the evidentiary record before this Court on judicial review of an administrative decision is restricted to the evidentiary record that was before the administrative decision maker (Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency (Access Copyright), 2012 FCA 22 at para 19 [Access Copyright]).

propositions.text: Exceptions to this rule exist but do not apply here (Access Copyright para 20).
propositions.quote: While there are exceptions to the general rule (Access Copyright at para 20), none apply in the present case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judicial review evidence is limited to record before decision maker; exceptions do not apply here.

propositions.text: Affidavit paragraphs 3 and 4 will not be considered; mootness is not an issue here.
propositions.quote: The information in paragraphs 3 and 4 of Ms. Bhatti’s affidavit will not be considered, however, I note Mr. Zeeshan’s concern about mootness and confirm that this is not at issue in the present matter.

paragraphs.summary: The court will not consider affidavit paragraphs 3 and 4 but confirms mootness is not an issue.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan did not qualify as dependent child under Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations as over 22 when father’s application filed.
propositions.quote: The Officer found that Mr. Zeeshan did not qualify as a “dependent child” as defined in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227, as he was over 22 years of age when his father’s application was filed.

propositions.text: Officer assessed Mr. Zeeshan’s request on H&C considerations under subsection 25(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the Officer assessed Mr. Zeeshan’s request on the basis of H&C considerations pursuant to subsection 25(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found Mr. Zeeshan was not a dependent child and assessed his request on H&C grounds under IRPA 25(1).

propositions.text: Exemption under IRPA 25(1) is exceptional, discretionary remedy (Fatt Kok, Huang).
propositions.quote: An exemption under subsection 25(1) of the IRPA is an exceptional and discretionary remedy (Fatt Kok v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 741 at para 7; Huang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 265 at paras 19-20).

propositions.text: IRPA 25(1) gives Minister broad discretion to exempt foreign nationals for H&C reasons.
propositions.quote: Subsection 25(1) of the IRPA confers broad discretion on the Minister to exempt foreign nationals from the ordinary requirements of that statute and to grant permanent resident status to an applicant in Canada if the Minister is of the opinion that such relief is justified by H&C considerations.

propositions.text: H&C discretion is flexible, equitable relief to mitigate law rigidity (Rainholz).
propositions.quote: The H&C discretion is a flexible and responsive exception that provides equitable relief, namely to mitigate the rigidity of the law in an appropriate case (Rainholz v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 121 at paras 13-14 [Rainholz]).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains IRPA 25(1) exemption is exceptional, discretionary, and equitable relief to mitigate law rigidity.

propositions.text: H&C considerations are facts that would excite reasonable person’s desire to relieve misfortunes warranting special relief (Kanthasamy).
propositions.quote: H&C considerations are facts, established by evidence, that would excite in a reasonable person in a civilized community the desire to relieve the misfortunes of another provided these misfortunes warrant the granting of special relief from the otherwise applicable provisions of the IRPA (Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 13, 21 [Kanthasamy]).

propositions.text: H&C hardship must be unusual, undeserved, and disproportionate to warrant exemption (Rainholz).
propositions.quote: Although not used in the statute itself, appellate case law has confirmed that the words ‘unusual’, ‘undeserved’ and ‘disproportionate’ describe the hardship contemplated by the provision that will give rise to an exemption” (Rainholz at para 15).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains H&C considerations require unusual, undeserved, disproportionate hardship warranting special relief.

propositions.text: H&C applicant bears onus to establish exemption is warranted; lack of evidence is at applicant’s peril (Rainholz).
propositions.quote: It is the H&C applicant, in this case Mr. Zeeshan, who bears the onus of establishing that an H&C exemption is warranted. Where there is a lack of evidence or a failure to adduce relevant information in support of such an application, this is at the peril of the applicant (Rainholz at para 18).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the H&C applicant bears the onus to prove exemption is warranted; lack of evidence is risky for applicant.

propositions.text: Officer accepted discrimination against Ahmadis in Pakistan but found insufficient evidence that Mr. Zeeshan’s situation warranted exemption.
propositions.quote: The Officer accepted that discrimination against the Ahmadi community occurs in Pakistan, but found that there was insufficient evidence that Mr. Zeeshan’s personal situation warranted an exemption.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan argues this finding is unreasonable given submitted materials and his father’s refugee status.
propositions.quote: Mr. Zeeshan pleads that this finding is unreasonable given the materials submitted from the National Documentation Package, the experiences of Mr. Zeeshan, and the fact that his father was granted refugee status on the basis of similar experiences.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan submits the Decision lacks a rational chain of analysis.
propositions.quote: Mr. Zeeshan submits that the Decision lacks the requisite rational chain of analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found insufficient evidence for exemption despite discrimination; Mr. Zeeshan argues this is unreasonable and lacks rational analysis.

propositions.text: Respondent submits Mr. Zeeshan’s argument is that Officer should have granted H&C once he was identified as Ahmadi.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that Mr. Zeeshan’s argument is effectively the following - once the Officer concluded he was Ahmadi, the Officer ought to have granted the H&C application.

propositions.text: Respondent highlights limited evidence and that cumulative factors did not meet threshold for exemption.
propositions.quote: The Respondent highlights that there was limited evidence in the record and the factors, when taken cumulatively, did not meet the threshold.

propositions.text: Respondent pleads Officer considered discrimination, education, living with siblings, and family network in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: The Respondent pleads that the factors taken into account by the Officer, in addition to the discrimination, included the fact that he was pursuing a university education, lives with his three older siblings, and has a family network in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Officer reasonably considered all factors and that evidence was limited, so exemption threshold was not met.

propositions.text: I am not persuaded that the Decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the Decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The test is not whether the Court would have arrived at the same conclusion as the Officer.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the test is not whether the Court would have arrived at the same conclusion as the Officer.

propositions.text: A Court must consider only whether the decision and reasoning process is reasonable, not decide the issue afresh (Vavilov at para 83).
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court has clearly stated that a Court is to refrain from deciding the issue afresh and instead must consider only whether the decision, including the decision maker’s reasoning process and the outcome is reasonable (Vavilov at para 83).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision reasonable, agrees with the Respondent on the test, and cites Vavilov on reasonableness review.

propositions.text: The Officer’s reasoning is rational and free of serious flaws, meeting the requirement of being justified, intelligible, and transparent.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the Officer’s reasoning can be followed without any serious flaws in its rationality or logic.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer’s reasoning rational and without serious flaws, meeting reasonableness standards.

propositions.text: The Officer did not specifically mention certain discrimination instances detailed in Mr. Zeeshan’s letter.
propositions.quote: I agree with Mr. Zeeshan that the Officer did not specifically mention certain instances of discrimination that Mr. Zeeshan detailed in his letter entitled “Supplementary Information (Update) IMM 5283” to the Officer.

propositions.text: This omission does not amount to a reviewable error when the Decision is read holistically.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, I do not find that this rises to the level of a reviewable error when the Decision is read holistically.

propositions.text: There is a presumption that a decision maker has considered all evidence before them (Burai v Canada, 2020 FC 966 at para 38).
propositions.quote: In addition, there is a presumption that a decision maker has weighed and considered all the evidence brought before them (Burai v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 966 at para 38).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer omitted discrimination details; court finds no reviewable error and cites presumption of consideration of all evidence.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan highlights his father’s refugee status to challenge the Decision’s reasonableness.
propositions.quote: While Mr. Zeeshan highlights that his father was granted refugee status,

propositions.text: Differences between Mr. Qureshi’s refugee claim and Mr. Zeeshan’s H&C application justify the Decision’s reasonableness.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that this is sufficient to render the Decision unreasonable. There are material differences in the legal and factual considerations between a claim for refugee status by Mr. Qureshi and the Officer’s assessment of Mr. Zeeshan’s H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant cites father’s refugee status; court finds material differences justify Decision’s reasonableness.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to consider all H&C factors, including family reunification and cultural dependence.
propositions.quote: I disagree with Mr. Zeeshan, that the Officer failed to apply the correct test by failing to consider all the H&C factors in play, notably reuniting him with his family, his cultural view that he is still a dependent, and the emotional and financial support his parents could provide.

propositions.text: The Officer mentioned Mr. Zeeshan’s cultural and financial dependence and addressed finances and family network.
propositions.quote: I find that the Officer specifically mentioned Mr. Zeeshan’s submissions that he was culturally and financially dependent on his parents, and then addressed the issue of finances and the family network with whom he resides.

propositions.text: Mr. Zeeshan’s argument is an impermissible request to reweigh evidence, which the court declines.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, I find Mr. Zeeshan’s argument on this point amounts to an impermissible request to reweigh the evidence considered by the Officer, which I decline.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer ignored H&C factors; court finds Officer considered them and declines to reweigh evidence.

propositions.text: The Officer’s reasons meet the reasonableness standard; the judicial review application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that the Officer’s reasons meet the standard of reasonableness set out in Vavilov.This application for judicial review is therefore dismissed.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance for certification arises.
propositions.quote: No serious question of general importance for certification was proposed by the parties, and I agree that no such question arises.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review and finds no serious question for certification.
